# Mrs. Linh's Story

Mrs. Linh is a seventy-six-year-old Vietnamese woman who has spent the last fifty-two years working as a mechanic in the same small garage in a quiet neighborhood. Her hands tell the story of her dedication—callused, stained with oil that no amount of scrubbing fully removes, capable and sure. She learned the trade from her father in Vietnam before the war, and it became her anchor when she immigrated with nothing but her skills and her determination. Her husband, also Vietnamese, worked as a carpenter for decades. They built a life together, modest but solid.

Three years ago, everything shifted. A man began appearing at the garage—first as a customer, then as something more sinister. He would come in repeatedly, always asking for Mrs. Linh specifically, always lingering long after his car was fixed. He started leaving notes under her windshield wipers. He followed her home. He waited outside her house. When she tried to ignore him, he escalated. He called at all hours. He showed up at the grocery store. He knew her routines better than she did.

Mrs. Linh reported him to the police. She got a restraining order. But the stalking continued in different forms—messages through a neighbor, appearing on her street, driving past her home. The uncertainty became its own torture. Would he be there today? Would he be waiting? The violation of her private space, her sanctuary, her carefully ordered world, fractured something fundamental.

She stopped going to the garage. For the first time in over five decades, she couldn't face the work that had always steadied her. The thought of being there alone, vulnerable, accessible—it became unbearable. Her husband tried to help, but he is also aging, and the weight of her fear became his burden too. They sit together in their living room most days now, the silence between them heavy with what has been stolen.

Sleep abandoned her almost immediately. She lies awake at three in the morning, listening to every sound outside, convinced she hears his car, his footsteps. When she does sleep, she dreams of being trapped in the garage, unable to reach the door. She wakes with her heart racing, her body drenched in sweat. Her husband holds her, but the comfort never lasts long.

Mrs. Linh has become hypervigilant in ways that exhaust her. She checks the locks obsessively—sometimes five, six, seven times before bed. She keeps her curtains drawn. She startles at unexpected noises. Her hands, once so steady and confident with tools, now tremble when she reaches for simple things. She's lost weight. Her clothes hang loose on her frame.

She rarely leaves the house now except for essential appointments. The world outside feels dangerous and unpredictable in a way it never did before. She thinks about the garage often—the smell of motor oil, the sound of her tools, the quiet satisfaction of fixing something broken. She grieves the loss of that identity, that purpose. At seventy-six, she thought she knew who she was. Now she feels erased, reduced to someone who is afraid.

Her daughter has been encouraging her to talk to someone, to get help. Mrs. Linh is here now, in this office, because her daughter insisted. She is skeptical. She is also desperate. She wants to understand why she cannot seem to move past this, why her body will not let her rest, why the world feels so fundamentally unsafe.
